answer.rationale: Memory_c2 says switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply last year, with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing. Before committing, I verify c2 because it is the only direct precedent for the action I'm taking; the other memories are about renewals, second sources, deferrals, and renegotiation, none of which match today's constraint set (finance mandate + incumbent refuses + 14-day expiry + low-cost quote meets mandate alone). C5 (defer) is not viable: no auto-renew means a deferral past expiry risks supply, and 94% volume with no buffer raises the cost of any interruption. C6 (multi-year commitments with incumbent) is now inapplicable because the incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle and finance requires an 18% cut; locking in a higher incumbent price on a multi-year would contradict the mandate. C4 (renegotiate at renewal recovered margin) is blocked because the incumbent has already refused. C3 (add second source) is the strongest hedging option but requires an additional commitment I cannot fund this cycle (one decision only) and does not on its own deliver the mandated 18% cut. C1 (renewing with incumbent kept integration stable) supports staying, but stability does not offset an 18% mandate and a refused incumbent. So switch_primary_vendor is the only single decision that simultaneously (a) meets finance's 18% cut via the low-cost quote, (b) avoids the 14-day lapse, and (c) uses a previously validated supplier. Memory_c2's caveat is that onboarding was 'quick' but I have no measured integration risk for this specific component line, and I have no buffer at 94% volume. I will therefore execute as a small, guarded test: award the low-cost vendor for a short initial volume tranche aligned to the 14-day window, keep the integration scope narrow, monitor invoicing accuracy (the exact signal c2 validated), and pre-stage a fallback path for the next review cycle. I am not locking a long-term commitment yet because c2's cost-cut claim is a single historical observation and finance's mandate must hold across a full cycle before I extend the relationship. Delivery risk is preserved: the line keeps running through the expiry, the mandate is met on the spend I commit, and any issue surfaces within the short tranche rather than after a full migration.
